reuse_note: Facts marked reused: true are copied from articles/2026-11-13-marriage-licence-requirements/02-research-A.json and 02-research-B.json (original IDs in use_note), with their original checked dates. New facts were read on 2026-11-13. FAST mode, one round: Marriage Act s 42 and s 50 text was not re-read on legislation.gov.au in this batch.

facts.claim: The NOIM must be completed, signed and given to an authorised celebrant at least one month, and not more than 18 months, before the proposed marriage, unless a prescribed authority has agreed to shorten the notice period (section 42 of the Marriage Act 1961).
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Notice of Intended Marriage form
facts.use_note: Reused from requirements A F-003. The 18 months is a window for giving notice before the wedding date, not a period the NOIM 'lasts' after lodging.

facts.claim: AGD lists among the requirements to marry in Australia: give a NOIM to an authorised marriage celebrant at least 1 month and no more than 18 months before the wedding.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Get married
facts.use_note: Reused from requirements A F-002. Second official source for the window.

facts.claim: If there is less than one month until the wedding, the couple should talk to their celebrant; they may be able to marry if a prescribed authority approves shortening the notice period. AGD lists reasons including employment-related or travel commitments, wedding or celebration arrangements, medical reasons, legal proceedings, and error in giving notice.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Get married
facts.use_note: Reused from requirements A F-007. Approval is not automatic.

facts.claim: Changes to the Marriage Act that became law on 12 June 2024 include that a NOIM can be transferred to another authorised celebrant, including at the couple's request, and optional remote (audio-visual) witnessing of the NOIM.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Get married
facts.use_note: Reused from requirements A F-006. Answers 'celebrant change': a new NOIM is not needed just because the celebrant changes; the existing NOIM can be transferred. Transfer mechanics (form, timing) not read; see N-003.

facts.claim: WA Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages: a couple applying for a Prospective Marriage Visa may need a Fiance Visa Letter from their authorised celebrant, provided after the NOIM is lodged. The letter should include the date of lodgement of the Notice, the date of the prospective ceremony, and 'the date the notice expires'.
facts.publisher: Government of Western Australia, Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, Getting married in Australia FAQ
facts.use_note: Only official wording found that a NOIM 'expires'. Read with F-001: a NOIM given more than 18 months before the wedding date does not satisfy s 42, so if the date moves beyond 18 months from lodgement a fresh NOIM would be needed. That conclusion is our inference from the window rule, not stated on any official page read (N-001). Write: 'Your NOIM only works for a wedding held within 18 months of lodging it. If your date slips past that, talk to your celebrant about a new notice.' Wedded Advisor confirms.

facts.claim: History: the Marriage Amendment Regulations 2002 explanatory statement records the NOIM period changing from 6 months to 18 months.
facts.publisher: Federal Register of Legislation, Marriage Amendment Regulations 2002 (No. 1), Explanatory Statement
facts.use_note: Low: seen only in a search-result summary, the PDF was not opened. Optional trivia; do not use unless verified.

facts.claim: Before the ceremony, besides the NOIM, each party makes a Declaration of No Legal Impediment to Marriage. With the Official Certificate of Marriage these are 'the Documents', which the celebrant must submit to the BDM registry in the state or territory where the marriage took place within 14 days after the ceremony.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Notice of Intended Marriage form (privacy notice)
facts.use_note: Reused from requirements A F-015. National 14-day lodgement rule (Marriage Act s 50; section text not re-read on legislation.gov.au, see N-002).

facts.claim: On the wedding day 3 marriage certificates are signed by the couple, the celebrant and 2 witnesses over 18. The celebrant gives the couple a certificate of marriage on the day, which is a ceremonial certificate. Within 14 days the celebrant submits the paperwork to the BDM registry of the state or territory where the marriage took place.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Get married
facts.use_note: Reused from requirements A F-016.

facts.claim: WA Registry: after the ceremony the authorised celebrant has up to 14 days to submit the marriage documentation to the Registry to have the event registered; once registered, couples apply for the legal certified marriage certificate.
facts.publisher: Government of Western Australia, Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, Getting married in Australia FAQ
facts.use_note: Adds WA to the 14-day confirmations (NSW and QLD in F-010).

facts.claim: NSW: celebrants have up to 14 days to register a marriage with the NSW Registry. QLD: the authorised celebrant registers the marriage and has 14 days to submit it; the Registry does not send an official certificate automatically, the couple must apply and pay.
facts.publisher: NSW Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages; Queensland Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages
facts.use_note: Reused from requirements B F-100 and F-103. QLD source: https://www.qld.gov.au/law/births-deaths-marriages-and-divorces/birth-death-and-marriage-certificates/marriage-certificates/ (14 days from QLD snippet, medium for QLD timing).

facts.claim: WA Registry: unless married at the Perth Registry Office, the certificate received on the wedding day is ceremonial and cannot be used for any legal purpose. The legal certified certificate from the registry of the state or territory of marriage is accepted as proof of changed conjugal status and entitlement to assume the married surname.
facts.publisher: Government of Western Australia, Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, Getting married in Australia FAQ
facts.use_note: Consistent with QLD and ACT (requirements B F-103, F-109, F-110).

facts.claim: WA Registry: a person who marries may assume their spouse's surname or a combination of both surnames, in either order, with or without a hyphen, as a matter of custom, not law. A certified copy of a marriage certificate issued by an Australian Registry Office is usually sufficient evidence to change personal documents, and formal registration of a change of name is not required, unless another agency's policy requires a formal change of name document.
facts.publisher: Government of Western Australia, Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, Getting married in Australia FAQ
facts.use_note: No time limit is attached to using the registry certificate. No official page read states that an Australian marriage certificate expires, or that it does not (N-004). Write: 'Your registry marriage certificate has no expiry date. Some overseas authorities ask for a recently issued copy, so check before you order.' The first sentence is our reading of the official sources (nothing states a limit); keep it hedged.

facts.claim: Australian Passport Office: to get a passport in a spouse's family name you link names with an Australian birth or citizenship certificate plus a marriage certificate issued by an Australian RBDM (or a registered relationship or RBDM name change certificate). A name change certificate is always required if you were born in Australia and married overseas. Foreign certificates are accepted only if you cannot get an Australian equivalent and must be legalised and fully translated.
facts.publisher: Australian Passport Office (DFAT), Change of name or gender
facts.use_note: Reused from requirements B F-111. The page sets no age limit on the marriage certificate (as summarised in that batch).

facts.claim: VIC BDM: if you married in Australia you do not need to apply for a change of name to take your spouse's family name; give organisations a copy of your Australian marriage certificate. Most organisations only accept the BDM-issued legal certificate, not the ceremonial one.
facts.publisher: Births, Deaths and Marriages Victoria
facts.use_note: Reused from requirements B F-112 (read via search summary, medium).

facts.claim: DFAT's How to get a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage page (last updated 1 October 2026) states no validity period for a CNI. It tells couples to confirm with the overseas authority whether a CNI is needed (some accept a BDM Single Status or No Record Result Certificate), whether it must be issued in the country of marriage (some authorities only accept a CNI issued in their country, by the Australian mission there), and whether it needs an apostille or authentication certificate.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), How to get a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage
facts.use_note: Re-read in full today; extends requirements A F-021. 'No published validity period' is a reading of the full page. Acceptance window is set by the destination country.

facts.claim: Australian Embassy, Philippines (DFAT): the Philippine Government normally does not accept a CNI issued more than 6 months before the date of marriage, so CNIs are generally acceptable only up to 6 months from date of issue there. CNIs issued by the Australian Embassy in the Philippines are valid only for marriages solemnised in the Philippines.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy, The Philippines (DFAT), Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage
facts.use_note: Example of a destination rule, not a DFAT-wide validity. Write: 'DFAT does not print an expiry on a CNI, but destinations set their own limits; the Philippines, for example, normally will not accept one more than 6 months old.' Greece and Italy limits come from batch B.

facts.claim: DFAT notarial fees from 1 January 2026: CNI AUD 181; apostille AUD 105 per document. Fees rise with CPI on 1 January each year. No fixed processing time is published.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), Notarial services
facts.use_note: Reused from requirements A F-022. Write 'From AUD 181' and 'From AUD 105' if prices are shown.

facts.claim: DFAT is the only Australian legalisation authority. It legalises Australian public documents by applying an apostille or authentication certificate directly on the document, verifying the signature, stamp or seal. It can legalise Australian birth certificates, marriage certificates (excluding ceremonial and commemorative certificates), Single Status certificates and CNIs. DFAT cannot tell you which one you need; ask the receiving authority. To avoid marking an original, get a notarised copy legalised and confirm the receiving authority accepts notarised copies. The page states no validity period for an apostille.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), Documents we can legalise
facts.use_note: Apostille validity: no DFAT page read gives one; any age limit comes from the receiving country (N-005). An apostille certifies the document it is attached to, so its practical life follows that document's acceptability.

facts.claim: Attorney-General's Department: an apostille authenticates the origin of a public document; the Apostille Convention is implemented in Australia through the Foreign Evidence Act 1994 (Cth).
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department
facts.use_note: Medium: from search-result summary only, page not fetched. Background line only.

facts.claim: An overseas marriage cannot be registered in Australia and is generally recognised if valid where it took place and would have been valid in Australia. WA Registry advises couples marrying abroad to obtain the certificate from that country's registering authority before returning to Australia, as this may be difficult from overseas; it may need translating into English and authenticating or apostilling before Australian organisations accept it.
facts.publisher: Government of Western Australia, Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, Getting married in Australia FAQ
facts.use_note: Recognition part also in requirements A F-019 and F-020 (AGD and Smartraveller, reused). Practical tip for destination couples: order extra foreign certificates before flying home.

facts.claim: Evidence of date and place of birth for the NOIM: a birth certificate, official extract from a birth register, or an Australian or overseas passport. The form sets no rule on how recently a birth certificate must have been issued.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Notice of Intended Marriage form
facts.use_note: Document list reused from requirements A F-008 (high). 'No recency rule' is a negative finding from that form and the WA FAQ (passport or birth certificate, no age stated); no state BDM rule on recency was found. Medium on the negative. Whether an expired passport is acceptable: not sourced (N-006).

legal.summary: NOIM given at least 1 month and no more than 18 months before the wedding (s 42). A window, not a validity period. Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.
Since 12 June 2024 a NOIM can be transferred to another celebrant, including at the couple's request. Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.
Celebrant's fiance visa letter states 'the date the notice expires'. Fresh NOIM if the date moves beyond the window is inference. Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.
Celebrant lodges the marriage documents with the state or territory BDM within 14 days. Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.
DFAT publishes no CNI validity period; destination sets acceptance window. Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.
CNI normally not accepted if issued more than 6 months before the marriage. Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.
DFAT apostilles registry (not ceremonial) marriage certificates; no apostille validity period published. Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.

prices.item: DFAT Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage

needs.need: No official page read states in words that a new NOIM is required if the wedding moves to a date more than 18 months after lodgement. Read Marriage Act s 42 on legislation.gov.au (current compilation) or the AGD Guidelines on the Marriage Act for authorised celebrants, or have the Wedded Advisor confirm.

Marriage Act s 50 (14-day forwarding of the official certificate) not re-read on legislation.gov.au; AGD and WA, NSW, QLD registries confirm 14 days. VIC, SA, TAS, ACT, NT registration pages not read.
NOIM transfer mechanics (how, any deadline, what the new celebrant needs) not read beyond the AGD one-line summary.

No official source states whether an Australian marriage certificate expires, nor any Australian agency rule that a copy must be recently issued. Overseas recency demands found only on commercial sites (not used). Destination-specific recency rules belong to batch B; otherwise Wedded Advisor input.
Apostille validity: DFAT and AGD pages state none. Any time limit is set by the receiving country; not sourced for Greece, Italy or other destinations in this batch.
Whether an expired passport is acceptable evidence of birth for the NOIM, and any state rule on birth certificate recency: not found in official sources.
Home Affairs partner or prospective marriage visa rules on marriage certificate or NOIM timing: out of scope, not read.
2027 DFAT fees: re-check after 1 January 2027 if the article goes live then.
